sections.overview: The edible frog is a green water frog of central and north-eastern Europe. It is not a true species in the usual sense but a fertile hybrid between the pool frog and the marsh frog, which keeps going by mating with one of its parents.
sections.identification: It reaches up to 12 cm but is mostly under 10 cm, females being larger. The back is light to dark green or brownish with dark spots, often with a light green stripe down the middle, and the backs of the thighs are yellowish or orange with dark bars. The skin is usually smooth and the hind legs long and well webbed. Males have grey nuptial pads on the thumbs and white to grey vocal sacs. The consulted species references do not provide a reliable adult body mass for identification; no weight is estimated here.
sections.habitat: It uses many sun-exposed waters with well-overgrown margins and shallows, from woodland ponds to ditches, lakes and rivers, sometimes in brackish water. It ranges across mid and north-eastern Europe as far as Russia. Introduced colonies in southern England probably all came from releases.
sections.diet: In mixed water frog populations studied in Serbia, insects made up about 88% of the prey items found in stomachs, mostly Hymenoptera, beetles, Lepidoptera and flies. Frogs are opportunistic hunters and their diet varies from site to site. It forages on land mainly at night.
sections.behavior: It stays mostly in water and basks a lot. It is mainly active by day but also at night during the breeding season, when males call in dense groups, chiefly in the evening, with grunting or rattling notes. It usually hibernates in soil on land, sometimes underwater, and young frogs can travel several kilometres.
sections.reproduction: Frogs leave hibernation from about mid-March and eggs are laid from April to mid-July, mostly around mid-May. A female lays 3,000 to 8,000 eggs per season. Tadpoles need two to four months to develop, most transforming between mid-August and mid-September, and frogs mature after two to three years.
sections.ecology: The edible frog reproduces by hybridogenesis: it passes on one parental genome unchanged and so needs a parent species to mate with. In the common arrangement it mates with the pool frog, in another with the marsh frog. Some populations are made up only of hybrids, with diploid and triploid frogs together.
sections.conservation: It is often the most numerous green frog where it occurs. The sources read give no Red List category for this hybrid. In Serbia, mixed populations of the three water frog forms are rare and only found along the Danube.
